unit.subject: English
unit.unitOverview: In this unit you will learn the words for shapes, colours and clothes. You will make things from paper shapes — a paper quilt, a picture, a shape animal. You will talk about what people are wearing, and dress up in pretend party costumes. You will meet the short 'e' sound in hen, pen and tent. Making things takes patience, and it is fun to try, try again.
unit.learningPath:
Begin with the guided teacher launch and learn a few words through pictures and play.
Listen to the Unit story and join in with repeated language.
Complete six language, speaking, early-writing and practical activities.
If you have access to live teacher sessions, meet your teacher three times each week for two weeks for extra practice — these are optional, and every skill in this unit is also fully covered through the teacher launch, story, and speaking and writing activities above.
Finish the ten-question checkpoint, then tell an adult what you can do if one is nearby — or say it out loud to yourself.

readings.title: Amal Makes a Mat
readings.setting: Home, online lesson or Grade 1 classroom
readings.passageScript: It was a warm afternoon in the village. Amal sat with her grandma under the big tree. Grandma was making a mat from soft grass. Her hands moved fast. Over, under, over, under. “I want to make a mat too!” said Amal. “Good,” said Grandma. “Here is some grass. We will make it together.” Amal took some grass. She started to weave. Over, under, over, under. But her mat was not neat. It was bumpy and full of holes. “Oh no!” said Amal. “My mat is not good.” Her big brother Adam walked by. He was carrying paper and crayons. “Do not be sad,” said Adam. “Look, I am making a picture with shapes. I cut a red circle and a blue square.” He showed Amal his paper. There was a green triangle and a yellow rectangle too. “It is beautiful,” said Amal. “But my first picture was not so good either!” said Adam. He laughed. “I tried again and again.” Amal looked at her bumpy mat. She took a deep breath. “I will try again,” she said. Over, under, over, under. Slow and careful this time. Amal did not rush. Little by little, the mat grew. The holes were gone. It was flat and neat. “Grandma, look!” said Amal. Grandma smiled a big smile. “You did it, Amal! You were patient. That is how we make good things.” Amal held up her mat. It was red and brown, like the earth. Her little sister Hodan clapped her hands. “I want to make a mat too!” “Come,” said Amal. “I will help you. Over, under, over, under…” And under the big tree, the whole family sat and made things together, all afternoon long.

readings.setting: Home, online lesson or Grade 1 classroom
readings.passageScript:
The “Party Time” poem — say it together
Party time, / Look at me. / What do you see? / I can be a clown / With a funny frown. / Or a king / With a silver ring.
Act it out! Make a funny frown for the clown. Put on a pretend crown for the king. Say it three times — a little sillier each time!
The “Higgledy Piggledy” rhyme — for the short ‘e’ sound
Higgledy Piggledy, / my black hen. / She lays eggs / for gentlemen. / Sometimes nine and sometimes ten.
Listen for the ‘e’ sound in hen, eggs, gentlemen and ten. Flap your arms like a hen while you say it!

grammar.title: Name your craft materials
grammar.explanation: Name one thing from your craft box. Say 'a' before most words, but 'an' before a vowel sound: a box, an apron.
grammar.commonMistake: Children pop 'a' before apron by mistake. Before an a, e, i, o, u sound we say 'an': an apron, an elastic band.
grammar.memoryTip: Open-mouth sound at the start — a, e, i, o, u — means you say 'an'.
grammar.practice: Name three craft things: This is a box. This is an apron. This is a straw.

grammar.title: Put the describing word first
grammar.explanation: The describing word comes first. Say 'a' or 'an' to match its sound: a big box, an old cloth.
grammar.commonMistake: Children pop 'a' before old by mistake. Before an a, e, i, o, u sound we say 'an': an old cloth, an empty tin.
grammar.memoryTip: Listen to the describing word. Open-mouth start — a, e, i, o, u — use 'an'.
grammar.practice: Describe three: It is a big box. It is an old cloth. It is a red straw.

grammar.title: Say what you are cutting
grammar.explanation: While you use your safe scissors, tell your teacher what you are cutting at this moment.
grammar.commonMistake: Some children say 'I cutting paper.' Keep 'am' in the middle: 'I am cutting paper.'
grammar.memoryTip: Snip two fingers like scissors as you say the word 'cutting'.
grammar.practice: Say three as you work: I am cutting paper. I am cutting card. I am cutting string.

grammar.title: Tell everyone what you are making
grammar.explanation: Show your work and say what it will be. Use this while you are still busy building it.
grammar.commonMistake: Children may say 'I making a card.' The small word 'am' belongs in every sentence like this.
grammar.memoryTip: Say it while your hands are still busy, because 'making' means not finished yet.
grammar.practice: Say three about your work: I am making a card. I am making a lantern. I am making a boat.

grammar.title: Say what you are wearing
grammar.explanation: Look down at your clothes today and say one thing you have on.
grammar.commonMistake: 'I am wearing a shoes' mixes 'a' with a plural. Say 'a shoe' for one and 'shoes' for two.
grammar.memoryTip: Touch each piece of clothing as you name it.
grammar.practice: Name three clothes you have on: I am wearing a shirt. I am wearing shoes. I am wearing a cap.

grammar.title: Say the job you dream of
grammar.explanation: Name a job you dream of. Say 'a' before most jobs, but 'an' before a vowel sound: a baker, an artist.
grammar.commonMistake: Children pop 'a' before artist by mistake. Before an a, e, i, o, u sound we say 'an': an artist, an engineer.
grammar.memoryTip: If the job word starts with an open-mouth sound — a, e, i, o, u — use 'an'.
grammar.practice: Say three jobs: I can be a baker. I can be an artist. I can be a teacher.

grownUpGuide.label: Teacher & Parent Guide
grownUpGuide.intro: In this unit, your child learns the words for shapes, colours, and clothes, and how to make things with paper shapes — like a paper quilt, a picture, or a shape animal. They talk about what people are wearing and dress up in pretend party costumes. They meet the short ‘e’ sound (hen, pen, tent) and enjoy the old story of the elves and the shoemaker. The gentle idea running through it all is that making things takes creativity and patience — and it is fun to try, try again.

sections.title: 🧭 About this unit (please read first)
sections.body:
Your child is a beginner, about 5–7 years old, and is just starting to read. So YOU lead this unit — a teacher in class or a parent at home.

Work in short, happy sessions of about 15–20 minutes. Lots of cutting, colouring, making, pointing, saying and singing — very little writing.

This guide tells you what to do. The Child Activity Sheet is what your child makes, draws and colours. The Story is one you read aloud.

Have some paper, safe scissors and crayons ready. This unit is all about making things with shapes and colours.

sections.title: 💬 Using the AI Tutor with a young child
sections.body:
The grown-up holds the device and reads with the child — do not leave a 5-year-old alone with it.

Ask the tutor to say a shape or colour word slowly so your child can copy the sound: “Please say the word ‘triangle’ slowly.”

Ask it to play a shape-guessing game: “I’m round with no corners — what shape am I?”

Ask it to sing the “London Bridge” song, or to help you make up a new colour verse.

Ask it to give you one more simple making idea if your child wants to keep going.

sections.title: 🌟 Tips for teaching absolute beginners
sections.body:
Keep it short and playful. Stop while it is still fun.

Making things can be messy — that is fine! The talking is what matters.

Repeat, repeat, repeat — young children learn by hearing words many times.

If a craft goes wrong, smile and say “Let’s try again!” Patience is part of the lesson.

Praise every try. Confidence matters more than being correct at this stage.

sections.title: Songs and Rhymes
sections.body:
The “Party Time” poem — say it together

Party time, / Look at me. / What do you see? / I can be a clown / With a funny frown. / Or a king / With a silver ring.

Act it out! Make a funny frown for the clown. Put on a pretend crown for the king. Say it three times — a little sillier each time!

The “Higgledy Piggledy” rhyme — for the short ‘e’ sound

Higgledy Piggledy, / my black hen. / She lays eggs / for gentlemen. / Sometimes nine and sometimes ten.

Listen for the ‘e’ sound in hen, eggs, gentlemen and ten. Flap your arms like a hen while you say it!

sections.title: How to Teach This Unit, Step by Step
sections.body:
Repeat this simple shape over several short sessions:

1. Warm-up (2–3 min)

Greet your child in English: “Hello! How are you today?”

Sing the “Party Time” poem together.

2. Learn the words (5 min)

Hold up a paper shape (or point to a picture) and say the word clearly: “circle”. Ask your child to repeat.

Do 4–5 words at a time — shapes one day, colours the next, clothes the next. Use big smiles and lots of praise.

3. Make and play (5 min)

Cut simple paper shapes together. As you cut, say: “I’m cutting a blue square.”

Make a little picture or paper quilt from the shapes. Say: “I’m making a picture.”

Play a Shape Hunt: “Find something round like a circle!” Your child points to or fetches it.

4. Story time (5 min)

Read the Story file, “Sagal Makes a Mat”, aloud. Point to the words in bold and to any pictures your child has drawn, and ask the simple talk-about questions.

5. Activity sheet (5 min)

Sit with your child and do one or two activities from the Child Activity Sheet. Read each instruction aloud for them. Making comes first — writing can be just a letter or a mark.

6. Wrap-up (2 min)

Ask: “What did we make today?” Celebrate! Say “Well done!” and one thing they did well.

sections.title: Sentence Patterns to Say Out Loud
sections.body: Speaking comes before writing. Practise these spoken patterns often:
items: “I’m cutting a ______.” (a red circle, a blue square)
“I’m making a ______.” (a picture, a quilt, a shape animal)
“This is a ______.” (a triangle, a rectangle)
“I’m wearing ______.” (a hat, a jacket)

sections.body: You do not need a test. Just watch and tick when your child can do these:
items: Points to and names 4 shapes (square, circle, triangle, rectangle).
Names 5 or more colours.
Says “I’m cutting ______.” and “I’m making a ______.”
Names 3 clothes and says “I’m wearing ______.”
Hears the short ‘e’ sound in hen, pen, ten.
Joins in the “Party Time” poem or a song.
